Geologists construct a geological time scale, a chronological record of Earth's history, based
on fossil types and radioactive dating. This scale divides geological history into six eras:
Archeozoic, Proterozoic, Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic, each characterized by specific
life forms, geological disturbances, and climatic changes.

Figure: 7.2.7 Evolution of horse The horse's genealogy stands as one of palaeontology's most extensively scrutinized. Commencing approximately 60 million years ago in the Eocene Epoch, the inaugural horse ancestor emerged. This creature, denoted scientifically as Hyracotherium but more commonly recognized as Eohippus or the 'dawn horse,' stood at around a foot in height, similar to a fox, and primarily consumed plants. Sporting 44 teeth, with moderately adapted cheeks for grinding, it exhibited four toes with a splint on the front foot and three toes with two splints on the hind foot. The ancestral lineage likely progressed through Eohippus, Mesohippus, Miohippus, Parahippus, Merychippus, and Pliohippus, culminating in the modern Equus, representative of contemporary horses. Throughout this evolutionary trajectory, following changes occurred to form the modern horse:

a. Increase in body size, b. Lengthening and increased mobility of the neck, c. Reduction in the number of toes from four to one, d. Elongation of the anterior portion of the skull, e. Extension of the distal parts of limbs, elevating the wrist and ankle, f. Specialization of teeth (molars and premolars) for grinding grasses, and g. Fusion of metatarsals and metacarpals
